title: The Path of the Just
hook: Moshe Chaim Luzzatto's 1740 ladder of traits

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: dan l'kaf zechut, judging on the side of merit. Your line was the benefit of the doubt. Whose story did you rewrite? Today, a book that turns the traits into a road. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-nine.

A book usually promises something new. This one opens by saying the opposite. Its author tells the reader, in effect: I haven't written this to teach you anything you don't know. I've written it to remind you of what you already know, and pass over every day. Then, chapter by chapter, he lays out a road, one trait leading to the next. Some Mussar students still study it, with a partner or alone. Today's word is its name.
screen: `NOTHING NEW, ON PURPOSE.` → `A REMINDER, NOT A DISCOVERY.` → `ONE TRAIT LEADS TO THE NEXT.`

segments.voice: Mesillat Yesharim. The path of the upright, or the path of the just. Turn it four ways. First, the author. Rabbi Moshe Chaim Luzzatto, a rabbi from Italy, known by his initials as the Ramchal. This is his short book on character. Second, the reminder. The introduction says the things in it are well known: everyone agrees that piety, humility, and the fear of Heaven matter. The trouble is that because they're so familiar, nobody stops to study them. People study what's hard and skip what's obvious, so the obvious never gets lived. His book is meant to slow a reader down on exactly those familiar things. Third, the ladder. Luzzatto didn't invent the order. He took it from a teaching of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair, preserved in the Talmud: Torah leads to watchfulness, watchfulness to zeal, zeal to cleanliness, cleanliness to separation, separation to purity, purity to piety, piety to humility, humility to fear of sin, fear of sin to holiness. Each rung rests on the one below it. You don't leap to holiness. You start by paying attention. Fourth, why a path. A path isn't a list; it has a first step and a direction. The traits this path has met over recent weeks, truth, trust, generosity, honor, guarded speech, stop being a pile of good ideas here and become a route. That's the shape the next days will follow, one rung at a time.
screen: `THE RAMCHAL, FROM ITALY.` · `TO REMIND, NOT TO TEACH.` · `RABBI PINCHAS BEN YAIR'S LADDER.` · `A ROUTE, NOT A PILE OF IDEAS.` · then, large: `THE PATH OF THE JUST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: climb one rung. Settle, and breathe. Think of your own character as a road, with you standing somewhere along it. Don't judge where. Just notice one good thing you already know you should be doing, something so familiar you've stopped seeing it. Calling a parent. Keeping a small promise. Saying thank you to someone you pass every day. Luzzatto's point is that the obvious is exactly what slips. Pick that one familiar thing, and see yourself doing it today, once, on purpose. That's the rung. If you pray, you can ask in your own words for help with the next step. The bell holds the time.
Mesillat Yesharim. The path of the just. Rabbi Moshe Chaim Luzzatto's book of traits, built as a ladder from watchfulness up to holiness. Today's word.
Your line: the path of the just. Today, do one good thing so familiar you've stopped noticing it, once, on purpose. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: Mussar students study Mesillat Yesharim, often a chapter at a time with a study partner or in a group, working through its traits in order from watchfulness toward holiness.

The Talmud's chain continues beyond holiness (ruach hakodesh, resurrection); confirm the list and that ending at holiness is fair for the book.
